Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?

By Ben Christopher, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.

It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.

It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country. 

There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37. 

Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.

Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers. 

Q: What would Proposition 37 do?

A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.

$25 billion? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget.

It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything. 

When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 and 38, would be paid back directly with tax dollars.

With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest. 

If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults. 

Are these loans just home mortgages?

Second mortgages, specifically.

Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.

That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?

Almost all of it. 

The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000. 

Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?

Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest or lowest homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it. 

For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn't going to help. 

But for some, it's the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey. The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.

Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview. 

Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?

He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California political debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.

Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.

If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?

If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible. 

Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters, according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis. 

Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify. 

There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income, first-generation or veteran homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said. 

But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California, worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.  

That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities. 

What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?

Two conditions apply.

First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.

Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.

Why only new homes?

This gets at a common critique of down payment assistance programs. 

Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.

Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.

Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.

How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?

It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.

To encourage the industry to build eligible homes, the measure includes a “qualified builder” option. If a builder agrees to abide by the measure’s price cap and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements, they’re shielded from construction defect lawsuits as long as they repair any future mistakes to a homeowner's satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.

The actual number of new units depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a whole bunch of other unknowns.

What other unknowns?

There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure. 

We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans. 

Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?

Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn't come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.

Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.

Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7%. Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.

Is this why buyers might not want to make use of these loans?

It’s the main reason.

Even if the second mortgage came with a 7% rate, that could add an extra $1,000 to a new homeowner’s monthly debt payments, depending on the price of the home. That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. Less than 40% of Prop. 37-eligible renters would be able to afford these higher monthly payments for an entry-level home, according to the PPIC analysis. 

For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.

Blog Post · October 7, 2026
How Many Might Actually Use the Down Payment Assistance in Proposition 37?
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
California’s homeownership rate is among the lowest in the nation—a full 10 percentage points below the average of all other states—and prices have spiraled beyond what many can afford. Yet for a large number of families, the down payment—not the monthly payment alone—is the wall they cannot climb. Proposition 37, a measure on the fall ballot, would offer a leg up to scale that wall. It would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to loan as much as 17% of a newly-built home’s purchase price for a down payment. Prop 37 is ambitious and could have a meaningful impact, but the challenges of California’s housing market and current interest rates will limit its reach.
The program has a high income ceiling: 200% of area median income, or in some locations up to $373,000 for a family of four in 2024, the most recent year with Census data. In that year, 91% of renters—the ones most likely to use the program—would have qualified. Qualification ran higher still among groups with the lowest ownership rates: 97% of renters without a high school degree, 93% of Black renters, and 95% of Latino renters.
The home price restriction is also generous. The sales price must fall below 125% of the county’s conforming loan limit—the ceiling on mortgages Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets each year and raises in high-cost counties. That would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024. While still falling short in some markets, that number would also have beat the statewide median (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAUCSFRCONDOSMSAMID) ($782,000 in December 2024) by roughly 50%.
But income eligibility is not purchasing power, and the math on buying has turned ugly. High prices are now paired with 7% interest rates (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/business/mortgage-rates-7-percent.html) that make a standard 30-year fixed loan with 20% down unaffordable for many. Capping monthly payments at 36% of monthly income (Fannie Mae’s maximum debt-to-income ratio), even an entry-level home at the lowest price range (defined here as the area’s 10 th percentile for new homes) would have been out of reach for 56% of California renters in 2024. Around the state, the median payment for such a home would have been $2,259, and as much as $4,195. One in four homeowners would have been unable to pay it.
Such costs erase much of Prop 37’s ability to address low homeownership rates among certain demographic groups. Among renters without a high school diploma, 71% could not have both qualified for Prop 37 and afforded an entry-level home in their area; three quarters of Black renters would have been in the same position. Latino renters were a partial exception: 39% cleared the bar, largely because they more often lived in lower-cost areas with incomes high enough to buy but still low enough for Prop 37.
Given these limitations, how many people could Prop 37 assist, and how would that compare to the number who might be ready for assistance? We don’t have data on wealth so we can’t say how many would be able to come up with money for a down payment. But setting that aside, if every loan went to a home at the maximum allowable price and drew the full 17% support, the program would have reached roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024—notable, though still far short of the more than one million units California is estimated to need (https://www.ppic.org/publication/housing-in-california/). If the state instead provided 5% of the maximum purchase price it would amount to 409,000 buyers. The full 17% applied to entry-level homes would be 560,000 buyers, and 5% support for entry-level would be 1.8 million. Buyers of cheaper homes will generally need more help, not less, so the 560,000 figure seems a reasonable central estimate that would provide full support for purchases at the low end of the market.
It is worth noting that subsidizing the highest-priced homes reaches farther as a share of potential buyers. The program’s $25 billion would be more than enough to cover the relatively small number of buyers qualifying at the maximum allowable sales price. Conversely, targeting lower prices expands the pool of potential buyers, but beyond what even $25 billion can reach.
Perhaps a better question is whether the program can help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. As of 2024, California needed to turn 1.35 million renters into homeowners to match the ownership rate in other states. The maximum 17% support for entry-level homes would have gotten the state about 41% of the way there. Maximum support for the maximum price would have barely made a dent (8%), while the lower five percent support for entry-level homes would have more than closed the gap (136%).
If Prop 37 passes, it will face additional barriers. Many renters would clearly fail to qualify for a conventional mortgage even with the down payment assistance, and many others might not be able to come up with any money for a down payment at all. Moreover, because the money must be spent on newly-built homes, the proposition’s success depends on builders expanding housing inventory.
At the same time, Prop 37’s $25 billion could meaningfully help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. The key will be to target, to the extent possible under the rules of the program, homes that are well below the maximum price allowed. Prop 37 might help Californians buy a home, but its dollars must spread across a larger number of lower-spending recipients to have the biggest effect.

Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?

By Ben Christopher, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.

It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.

It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country. 

There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37. 

Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.

Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers. 

Q: What would Proposition 37 do?

A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.

$25 billion? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget.

It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything. 

When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 and 38, would be paid back directly with tax dollars.

With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest. 

If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults. 

Are these loans just home mortgages?

Second mortgages, specifically.

Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.

That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?

Almost all of it. 

The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000. 

Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?

Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest or lowest homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it. 

For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn't going to help. 

But for some, it's the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey. The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.

Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview. 

Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?

He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California political debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.

Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.

If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?

If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible. 

Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters, according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis. 

Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify. 

There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income, first-generation or veteran homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said. 

But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California, worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.  

That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities. 

What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?

Two conditions apply.

First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.

Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.

Why only new homes?

This gets at a common critique of down payment assistance programs. 

Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.

Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.

Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.

How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?

It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.

To encourage the industry to build eligible homes, the measure includes a “qualified builder” option. If a builder agrees to abide by the measure’s price cap and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements, they’re shielded from construction defect lawsuits as long as they repair any future mistakes to a homeowner's satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.

The actual number of new units depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a whole bunch of other unknowns.

What other unknowns?

There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure. 

We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans. 

Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?

Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn't come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.

Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.

Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7%. Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.

Is this why buyers might not want to make use of these loans?

It’s the main reason.

Even if the second mortgage came with a 7% rate, that could add an extra $1,000 to a new homeowner’s monthly debt payments, depending on the price of the home. That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. Less than 40% of Prop. 37-eligible renters would be able to afford these higher monthly payments for an entry-level home, according to the PPIC analysis. 

For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.

Is there anything the state could do to bring these interest rates down?

Public money isn’t supposed to subsidize or backstop these loans, so not directly.

**California 2026 Proposition 37 (November 3, 2026): "Creates a loan program for middle-income buyers of qualifying new homes. Initiative statute."**

Mechanism:
- Allows CalHFA (California Housing Finance Agency) to sell up to $25 billion in **revenue bonds** (not general obligation bonds — not backed by the state's taxing authority, and the state is not on the hook for repayment).
- Uses the proceeds for a new "Middle-Class Homeownership Loan" program: fixed-rate second mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price of qualifying new homes (newly built or newly converted. Buyers must be first purchasers. Price cap of 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, i.e., roughly $1M in inland areas to about $1.5M in coastal areas).
- Buyer requirements: CA resident for 1+ year, primary residence, household income at or below 200% of area median income, at least 3% cash down payment.
- Bonds are repaid by homebuyers' loan payments + interest. The LAO (Legislative Analyst's Office) notes no direct state or local costs.
- "Qualified Builder" option: Builders that agree to the price caps and labor standards get more lenient construction defect rules (protection from construction defect lawsuits as long as they make the homeowner satisfied with repairs. Legal fees capped if litigation goes to court).
- CalHFA has discretion on how much of the $25 billion to issue and when. The state is not obligated to implement the program.

Key facts / points of contention:

For (YES):
1. **No direct taxpayer cost**: LAO estimates zero direct state or local costs. Revenue bonds repaid by borrower payments. If the program fails to attract investors or borrowers, CalHFA simply issues fewer bonds — the downside is limited (California Budget & Policy Center's Chris Hoene: "If it doesn't work, the state isn't really on the hook").
2. **Addresses an actual barrier**: California has the lowest (or second-lowest) homeownership rate in the nation. Down payments are the biggest hurdle for many middle-income families. The program lowers the required cash down payment to 3%.
3. **Promotes new construction**: By restricting it to new homes, the program theoretically aligns new demand with new supply, and could spur construction (the campaign's analysis estimates up to 190,000 homes, though that's the upper bound. PPIC's central estimate is that the funds could cover on the order of 560,000 buyers purchasing entry-level homes with full support — but the $25 billion is finite).
4. **Broad eligibility**: About 90% of renters qualify by income (PPIC).
5. **Breadth of support**: Governor Newsom, unions (including carpenter unions), state Realtor association, mayors, SPUR (yes vote), the California Budget & Policy Center is lukewarm, and even PPIC's survey shows the most strongly "yes" stance on the ballot (61–35 per a master guide citing PPIC's September poll — actually this cites a PPIC September survey showing 61% in favor, 35% opposed — "the strongest position on the ballot").
6. No official opposition argument has been submitted. No opposition committee was formed.

Against (NO):
1. **Debt burden / unaffordability**: Second mortgages at higher interest rates (7%+ for a primary mortgage, likely higher for riskier subprime second mortgages) add roughly $900–$1,000/month to the payment. PPIC: fewer than 40% of eligible renters can afford the higher payment on an entry-level home, and less than 0.5% can afford it at the maximum price. 56% of renters can't afford even an entry-level home's payments at 2024 interest rates.
2. **Demand-side stimulus could push up prices / benefit those who need help the least**: LWVC (League of Women Voters) is against, concerned about increased debt and opacity. Critics argue the most likely beneficiaries are higher-income households near the income cap or those with family support — reinforcing racial/economic disparities.
3. **Uncertain investor appetite**: Second mortgages without GSE (Fannie/Freddie) backing carry high rates. If rates are high, few buyers will use the program, and the program may be a dud. Hertzberg's plan relies on philanthropists buying bonds below market (a "war bonds"-style appeal), which is unproven.
4. **Doesn't address root causes** (construction costs, monthly mortgage burden). Critics: Mercury News editorial, San Diego Union-Tribune editorial (both call for rejection), KPBS.
5. **Political bailout risk**: Some analysts doubt that in the event of a wave of defaults, the legislature could resist bailing out homebuyers (potential future taxpayer exposure despite the "no direct cost").
6. **Builder quid pro quo**: The "Qualified Builder" option grants legal protections (reduced construction defect liability) in exchange for price caps and labor standards. Critics see this as a sweetheart deal with the construction industry. The construction defect protections are softened if a builder sells above the cap (25% over).
7. **Lack of transparency on loan terms**: Interest rates, repayment terms, and eligibility details are set post-vote by CalHFA.

Vote forecast / public opinion: PPIC's September 2026 survey shows 61% in favor, 35% opposed. It's expected to pass comfortably (like 2020's Prop 13/14).

My judgment framework: The user is asking for a yes/no recommendation. Key decision considerations:
- Downside risk to the voter/taxpayer: essentially zero by design (revenue bonds, CalHFA discretion, no General Fund cost). Even the most skeptical left-leaning analyst (Chris Hoene) says "if it doesn't work, the state isn't really on the hook."
- Upside potential: meaningful — if it works, it could help hundreds of thousands of middle-income buyers purchase new homes, and could spur new construction (up to 190,000 homes per the campaign's upper-bound estimate. PPIC: even at 17% on entry-level homes, it could help about 41% close the homeownership gap. At 5% on entry-level, more than 100%).
- The main criticism (increasing debt) applies to the program's users, not to the voters. Users voluntarily opt in. The program can't force anyone into a loan.
- The biggest structural risk is that the program doesn't materialize (investor rates too high) — but even then the taxpayer cost is near zero.
- There are concerns about a builder quid pro quo, but the labor standards requirements (training for workers on certain projects) partially offset this, and the construction defect flexibility is limited to qualified builders and is conditioned on satisfying price caps and repairs.

Given the limited downside to the public + potential for large upside + PPIC polling at 61% in favor + endorsements from the Governor, unions, and SPUR, a rational vote-advice call is: **YES**.

- "Qualified Builder" labor standards: "Workers of a certain type of training must be used for certain types of housing projects" — let me quickly verify the specifics in the bill text (e.g., prevailing wage? registered apprentices?). This is a notable provision — the carpenter unions support it, suggesting a labor benefits angle.

Just one more check: the details of the "Qualified Builder" labor standards in the bill text PDF might be important. But given time constraints, the information I have is sufficient to reach a conclusion.

Actually, let me reconsider the concerns a bit more carefully:

1. Bailout risk: The LAO analysis says no direct state or local costs. But critics point out that if there's a wave of defaults, there could be future political pressure for a bailout. This is a real but contingent risk. Also, since CalHFA has to "keep interest costs to homebuyers as low as possible," could CalHFA potentially seek a state subsidy? The bill probably prohibits state guarantees. CalMatters: "Public funds cannot directly subsidize or backstop these loans." OK.

2. Who benefits? The program is broadly available (income cap of 200% AMI is generous). The concern that the wealthiest within that band benefit the most has some validity, but SPUR and others argue that expanding homeownership helps overall, and homeownership is a primary channel of wealth building for middle-income households. Critics argue the most likely beneficiaries are higher-income households near the income cap or those with family support — reinforcing racial/economic disparities.
3. **Uncertain investor appetite**: Second mortgages without GSE (Fannie/Freddie) backing carry high rates. If rates are high, few buyers will use the program, and the program may be a dud. Hertzberg's plan relies on philanthropists buying bonds below market (a "war bonds"-style appeal), which is unproven.
4. **Doesn't address root causes** (construction costs, monthly mortgage burden). Critics: Mercury News editorial, San Diego Union-Tribune editorial (both call for rejection), KPBS.
5. **Political bailout risk**: Some analysts doubt that in the event of a wave of defaults, the legislature could resist bailing out homebuyers (potential future taxpayer exposure despite the "no direct cost").
6. **Builder quid pro quo**: The "Qualified Builder" option grants legal protections (reduced construction defect liability) in exchange for price caps and labor standards. Critics see this as a sweetheart deal with the construction industry. The construction defect protections are softened if a builder sells above the cap (25% over).
7. **Lack of transparency on loan terms**: Interest rates, repayment terms, and eligibility details are set post-vote by CalHFA.

Vote forecast / public opinion: PPIC's September 2026 survey shows 61% in favor, 35% opposed. It's expected to pass comfortably (like 2020's Prop 13/14).

- Downside risk to the voter/taxpayer: essentially zero by design (revenue bonds, CalHFA discretion, no General Fund cost). Even the most skeptical left-leaning analyst (Chris Hoene) says "if it doesn't work, the state isn't really on the hook."
- Upside potential: meaningful — if it works, it could help hundreds of thousands of middle-income buyers purchase new homes, and could spur new construction (up to 190,000 homes per the campaign's upper-bound estimate. PPIC: even at 17% on entry-level homes, it could help about 41% close the homeownership gap. At 5% on entry-level, more than 100%).
- The main criticism (increasing debt) applies to the program's users, not to the voters. Users voluntarily opt in. The program can't force anyone into a loan.
- The biggest structural risk is that the program doesn't materialize (investor rates too high) — but even then the taxpayer cost is near zero.
- There are concerns about a builder quid pro quo, but the labor standards requirements (training for workers on certain projects) partially offset this, and the construction defect flexibility is limited to qualified builders and is conditioned on satisfying price caps and repairs.

Given the limited downside to the public + potential for large upside + PPIC polling at 61% in favor + endorsements from the Governor, unions, and SPUR, a rational vote-advice call is: **YES**.

Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. ***Construction Defect Law.*** To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction.
Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards.

Prop 37’s construction-defect fix is designed to support union labor.
Only developers who opt into the “qualified builder” track get the more builder-friendly rules: a stronger right to repair, releases after those repairs, and less long-tail lawsuit risk.
That track requires higher labor standards that, in practice, run through union apprenticeship pipelines.
Why not just fix those construction-defect rules for everyone, so homes can be built more cheaply across California without favoritism?
Prop 37 keeps the rules in place to incentivized developers to walk hand in hand with the trade unions.
...
Nothing that makes California housing so expensive is removed with Prop 37.
The state can continue to layer long permit times, high construction costs, delays and a defect-liability regime that has crushed condominium production.
Publicly assisted housing already shows what those rules cost: studies find affordable and tax-credit projects run 1.2 to 1.5 times market-rate housing inside California; prevailing-wage requirements on that kind of work have been associated with $83,000 to $94,000 in added cost per unit.
Proposition 37 does not impose those wage rules on *new* second-mortgage homes, and it does not repeal them anywhere else.

Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. I now have a comprehensive overall picture. Let me organize the research findings.

**California 2026 Proposition 37 (November 3, 2026): "Creates a loan program for middle-income buyers of qualifying new homes. Initiative statute."**

Mechanism:
- Allows CalHFA (California Housing Finance Agency) to sell up to $25 billion in **revenue bonds** (not general obligation bonds — not backed by the state's taxing authority, and the state is not on the hook for repayment).
- Uses the proceeds for a new "Middle-Class Homeownership Loan" program: fixed-rate second mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price of qualifying new homes (newly built or newly converted. Buyers must be first purchasers. Price cap of 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, i.e., roughly $1M in inland areas to about $1.5M in coastal areas).
- Buyer requirements: CA resident for 1+ year, primary residence, household income at or below 200% of area median income, at least 3% cash down payment.
- Bonds are repaid by homebuyers' loan payments + interest. The LAO (Legislative Analyst's Office) notes no direct state or local costs.
- "Qualified Builder" option: Builders that agree to the price caps and labor standards get more lenient construction defect rules (protection from construction defect lawsuits as long as they make the homeowner satisfied with repairs. Legal fees capped if litigation goes to court).
- CalHFA has discretion on how much of the $25 billion to issue and when. The state is not obligated to implement the program.

Key facts / points of contention:

For (YES):
1. **No direct taxpayer cost**: LAO estimates zero direct state or local costs. Revenue bonds repaid by borrower payments. If the program fails to attract investors or borrowers, CalHFA simply issues fewer bonds — the downside is limited (California Budget & Policy Center's Chris Hoene: "If it doesn't work, the state isn't really on the hook").
2. **Addresses an actual barrier**: California has the lowest (or second-lowest) homeownership rate in the nation. Down payments are the biggest hurdle for many middle-income families. The program lowers the required cash down payment to 3%.

Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

I've done extensive research at this point. Let me summarize everything I know about California's 2026 Proposition 37:

**What it is**: An initiative statute (California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026), authored by former State Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg, qualified via a petition (over 900,000 signatures).

**What it does**:
1. Allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in **revenue bonds** (not general obligation bonds).
2. Uses the funds to establish a "Middle-Class Homeownership Loan" — a fixed-rate second mortgage covering up to 17% of the purchase price of a "qualified new home" (new construction or first sale of a converted non-residential building; price cap of 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, roughly $1M–$1.5M).
3. Borrower requirements: CA resident for 1+ year, primary residence, income at or below 200% of area median income (AMI), minimum 3% cash down payment. Together with the 17% loan, this effectively achieves 20% down payment and avoids private mortgage insurance (PMI).
4. Bonds are repaid solely by homebuyer loan payments + interest; **no direct state or local cost** (LAO).
5. CalHFA has discretion over the timing and amount of bond issuance; the state is not obligated to implement the program.
6. Voluntary "Qualified Builder" option: builders that agree to higher labor standards (prevailing wage, apprenticeship, contractor registration, payroll reporting on buildings over 85 feet; incorporating PRC §21080.66 provisions from the 2025 infill housing law) receive more flexible construction defect procedures (enhanced right to cure, releases, fee caps, including 30% cap on contingency fees). The benefit is lost if any unit is sold more than 25% above the cap.

**Fiscal analysis (LAO)**: No direct state or local cost. Uncertainties: investor demand/rates; loan utilization; whether it spurs construction and homebuying.

**Supporters**: Gov. Newsom; UNAC (nurses), California Conference of Carpenters, State Treasurer Fiona Ma (signatories on the ballot argument); California Association of Realtors (largest funder: roughly $18.4M), National Association of Realtors, Building a Better California (Sergey Brin/John Doerr, $6M), carpenters unions ($1.7M+), labor unions (CLC, State Building and Construction Trades, CFT, CTAs, etc.), mayors, SPUR (yes vote). No opposing argument submitted; no opposition committee. Total yes-side fundraising about $28–33.6M.

**Opponents/Critics**: League of Women Voters of California (against — debt burden, opaque terms); Mercury News editorial (against); San Diego Union-Tribune editorial (against); OC Register editorial (against — "risky $25B experiment"); Hoover Institution's analysis; AEI's Edward Pinto (second mortgages will have high interest rates); KPBS (state shouldn't be in the mortgage business; doesn't address root causes); California Current (op-ed: "Robin Hood in reverse"; favors union labor).

**Main criticisms**:
1. Adds debt: second mortgages at rates likely above 7% add about $900–1,000/month; PPIC: fewer than 40% of eligible renters can afford entry-level payments, under 0.5% can afford at the price cap.
2. Uncertain investor appetite for unsecured second-mortgage bonds → high rates or thin market; the program may not deliver much.
3. Demand-side stimulus may push up new-home prices / benefit those who need help the least; racial/equity concerns (LWVC, SPUR's note on equity).
4. Doesn't address the root cause (construction costs, monthly mortgage burden).
5. Political bailout risk if there are widespread defaults (Hoover's analysis; CalMatters mentions doubts).
6. Builder quid pro quo (construction defect protection) is criticized as favorable to industry/unions.
7. Loan terms (rates, repayment) determined after the vote — opaque.

**Main benefits**:
1. No taxpayer cost; downside is limited (if it fails to work, no bond issuance; "state is not actually on the hook" — California Budget & Policy Center).
2. California has the lowest/second-lowest homeownership rate in the nation; down payment is the biggest barrier for middle-income households; roughly 90% of renters are income-eligible (PPIC).
3. Limited to new construction → new supply matches new demand (mitigates the "musical chairs" criticism of demand-side-only down payment assistance); potential to spur construction (up to 190,000 units per campaign analysis, an upper bound).
4. If the program is well designed (e.g., full 17% on entry-level homes), PPIC suggests it could help 560,000 buyers and get the state about 41% of the way to closing the homeownership gap; a 5% subsidy could close more than 100% of the gap.
5. Public opinion: PPIC September 2026 poll: 61% yes / 35% no — strongest favorability of any proposition on the ballot.
6. 3% down payment requirement maintains some skin-in-the-game; 20% total equity avoids PMI.
7. Annual independent audit requirement.

**Decision**:
- Public downside: essentially zero (revenue bonds, state not on the hook, CalHFA discretion).
- Upside: potentially very large (tens to hundreds of thousands of new homeowners; spurs new construction).
- The "harm" critique mainly concerns individual borrowers who voluntarily opt in, not the voters.
- Even the skeptics' view: even if the program is a dud, the taxpayer cost is minimal; the "bailout" scenario is a contingent future political risk, but the bonds' structure is designed to avoid it.
- Strong endorsement base, broad middle-class appeal, no organized opposition.

Conclusion: **YES**.

## Case for YES (what the research shows)
- **Near-zero downside for taxpayers.** This is the pivotal fact. It's structured as a pass-through: CalHFA borrows from private bondholders and relends. No argument against was even submitted, and no opposition committee exists.

## Case for NO (the legitimate critiques)
- **Adds leverage, not affordability.** The second mortgage likely prices above the already ~7%+ primary rate; PPIC finds <40% of eligible renters could afford the higher payments on an entry-level home, and <0.5% at the price cap. - **The builder quid pro quo** (defect-liability relief for labor-standards compliance) reads as industry-favoring.

**Main criticisms**:
1. Adds debt: second mortgages at rates likely above 7% add about $900–1,000/month; PPIC: fewer than 40% of eligible renters can afford entry-level payments, under 0.5% can afford at the price cap.

7. Loan terms (rates, repayment) determined after the vote — opaque.

**Decision**:
- Public downside: essentially zero (revenue bonds, state not on the hook, CalHFA discretion).
- Upside: potentially very large (tens to hundreds of thousands of new homeowners; spurs new construction).
- The "harm" critique mainly concerns individual borrowers who voluntarily opt in, not the voters.
- Even the skeptics' view: even if the program is a dud, the taxpayer cost is minimal; the "bailout" scenario is a contingent future political risk, but the bonds' structure is designed to avoid it.
- Strong endorsement base, broad middle-class appeal, no organized opposition.

Conclusion: **YES**.

5. Public opinion: PPIC September 2026 poll: 61% yes / 35% no — strongest favorability of any proposition on the ballot.
6. 3% down payment requirement maintains some skin-in-the-game; 20% total equity avoids PMI.
7. Annual independent audit requirement.

**Decision**:
- Public downside: essentially zero (revenue bonds, state not on the hook, CalHFA discretion).
- Upside: potentially very large (tens to hundreds of thousands of new homeowners; spurs new construction).
- The "harm" critique mainly concerns individual borrowers who voluntarily opt in, not the voters.
- Even the skeptics' view: even if the program is a dud, the taxpayer cost is minimal; the "bailout" scenario is a contingent future political risk, but the bonds' structure is designed to avoid it.
- Strong endorsement base, broad middle-class appeal, no organized opposition.

Conclusion: **YES**.

I've done extensive research on this one. First, an important identification: that URL is the **2026 California General Election (Nov. 3, 2026) Proposition 37 — "Creates Loan Program for Middle‑Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes"** (the "California Middle‑Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act," authored by former Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg). It is *not* the 2012 GMO-labeling measure that once lived at a similar URL.

## What it actually does
- Lets the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) sell up to **$25 billion in revenue bonds** (not General Obligation bonds) and use the proceeds to lend homebuyers **up to 17% of the price of a newly built home** as a fixed-rate second mortgage.
- Buyers must: be CA residents ≥1 year, occupy the home as a primary residence, earn ≤200% of area median income (~$116K in Imperial County up to ~$410K in San Mateo for a family of 3), and put down **at least 3% cash**. The 17% loan + 3% cash ≈ 20% equity, avoiding PMI.
- Homes must be **new construction or first sale of converted nonresidential property** (no resales), priced at ≤125% of the county's conforming loan limit (~$1M–$1.5M).
- **Bonds are repaid by homeowners' loan payments and interest, not taxpayers.** The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) finds **no direct state or local cost**. CalHFA decides how much (if any) of the $25B to issue — the state has no obligation to run the program.
- A voluntary "qualified builder" option trades higher labor standards (prevailing wage, apprenticeship, contractor registration for certain projects) for more flexible construction-defect procedures.

## Case for YES (what the research shows)
- **Near-zero downside for taxpayers.** This is the pivotal fact. It's structured as a pass-through: CalHFA borrows from private bondholders and relends. If investors won't buy the bonds at reasonable rates, or buyers don't take the loans, CalHFA simply issues less. Even skeptical left-leaning analysts concede the point (Chris Hoene, California Budget & Policy Center: "If it doesn't work, the state's not really on the hook").
- **Targets a real, documented barrier.** California has the lowest (or 2nd lowest) homeownership rate in the nation — ~10 points below the national average. PPIC finds ~90% of renters are income-eligible, and the down payment (not monthly payments) is the wall for many middle-income families.
- **New-construction restriction is a genuine design strength.** Unlike ordinary down-payment assistance (which is often just "musical chairs"), limiting loans to new units pairs new demand with new supply — potentially adding thousands to tens of thousands of homes (campaign analysis: up to ~190,000, high-end).
- **PPIC's math suggests meaningful upside:** full 17% support on entry-level homes could reach ~560,000 buyers and get the state ~40% of the way to closing the homeownership gap; modest 5% support on entry-level homes could exceed 100%.
- **Strong, broad coalition:** Gov. Newsom, statewide unions (carpenters, CFT, CLC, nurses), the California and National Associations of Realtors (≈$25M+ in contributions), mayors, SPUR ("Vote YES"), and the **strongest public support of any 2026 proposition in the PPIC poll (61% yes / 35% no)**. No argument against was even submitted, and no opposition committee exists.

## Case for NO (the legitimate critiques)
- **Adds leverage, not affordability.** The second mortgage likely prices above the already ~7%+ primary rate; PPIC finds <40% of eligible renters could afford the higher payments on an entry-level home, and <0.5% at the price cap. Mercury News/San Diego U-T editorials: "Californians can't borrow their way out of a housing crisis."
- **Distribution risk.** The League of Women Voters of California (the main institutional opponent) argues the most likely users are higher-income, wealthier households near the cap — potentially reinforcing racial/economic disparities.
- **Market uncertainty.** AEI's Edward Pinto and others note second mortgages carry a big risk premium without Fannie/Freddie backing; if rates are high, the program may be a dud. Hertzberg's fallback plan (philanthropists buying bonds below market) is unproven.
- **Contingent bailout risk:** a few analysts doubt the Legislature would resist bailing out homebuyers in a wave of defaults, despite the "no state cost" structure.
- **The builder quid pro quo** (defect-liability relief for labor-standards compliance) reads as industry-favoring.

## My verdict
The decisive comparison is risk allocation: the measure imposes **essentially no financial obligation on the state or taxpayers** (revenue bonds only, CalHFA discretion, no General Fund commitment), while creating an **opt-in tool** that — if investor rates work out — could genuinely expand middle-class homeownership and new-construction supply in the state with the worst homeownership rate in the country. The main criticisms (more borrower debt, possible windfalls to higher earners, industry-friendly builder provisions) fall on voluntary participants or are secondary to the structural point that a "No" vote costs the state nothing and a "Yes" vote costs the state nothing but creates a chance of large public benefit. That asymmetric risk/reward profile is hard to vote against.

**Yes.**

How Many Might Actually Use the Down Payment Assistance in Proposition 37?
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
California’s homeownership rate is among the lowest in the nation—a full 10 percentage points below the average of all other states—and prices have spiraled beyond what many can afford. Yet for a large number of families, the down payment—not the monthly payment alone—is the wall they cannot climb. Proposition 37, a measure on the fall ballot, would offer a leg up to scale that wall. It would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to loan as much as 17% of a newly-built home’s purchase price for a down payment. Prop 37 is ambitious and could have a meaningful impact, but the challenges of California’s housing market and current interest rates will limit its reach.
The program has a high income ceiling: 200% of area median income, or in some locations up to $373,000 for a family of four in 2024, the most recent year with Census data. In that year, 91% of renters—the ones most likely to use the program—would have qualified. Qualification ran higher still among groups with the lowest ownership rates: 97% of renters without a high school degree, 93% of Black renters, and 95% of Latino renters.
The home price restriction is also generous. The sales price must fall below 125% of the county’s conforming loan limit—the ceiling on mortgages Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets each year and raises in high-cost counties. That would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024. While still falling short in some markets, that number would also have beat the statewide median (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAUCSFRCONDOSMSAMID) ($782,000 in December 2024) by roughly 50%.
But income eligibility is not purchasing power, and the math on buying has turned ugly. High prices are now paired with 7% interest rates (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/business/mortgage-rates-7-percent.html) that make a standard 30-year fixed loan with 20% down unaffordable for many. Capping monthly payments at 36% of monthly income (Fannie Mae’s maximum debt-to-income ratio), even an entry-level home at the lowest price range (defined here as the area’s 10 th percentile for new homes) would have been out of reach for 56% of California renters in 2024. Around the state, the median payment for such a home would have been $2,259, and as much as $4,195. One in four homeowners would have been unable to pay it.
Such costs erase much of Prop 37’s ability to address low homeownership rates among certain demographic groups. Among renters without a high school diploma, 71% could not have both qualified for Prop 37 and afforded an entry-level home in their area; three quarters of Black renters would have been in the same position. Latino renters were a partial exception: 39% cleared the bar, largely because they more often lived in lower-cost areas with incomes high enough to buy but still low enough for Prop 37.
Given these limitations, how many people could Prop 37 assist, and how would that compare to the number who might be ready for assistance? We don’t have data on wealth so we can’t say how many would be able to come up with money for a down payment. But setting that aside, if every loan went to a home at the maximum allowable price and drew the full 17% support, the program would have reached roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024—notable, though still far short of the more than one million units California is estimated to need (https://www.ppic.org/publication/housing-in-california/). If the state instead provided 5% of the maximum purchase price it would amount to 409,000 buyers. The full 17% applied to entry-level homes would be 560,000 buyers, and 5% support for entry-level would be 1.8 million. Buyers of cheaper homes will generally need more help, not less, so the 560,000 figure seems a reasonable central estimate that would provide full support for purchases at the low end of the market.
It is worth noting that subsidizing the highest-priced homes reaches farther as a share of potential buyers. The program’s $25 billion would be more than enough to cover the relatively small number of buyers qualifying at the maximum allowable sales price. Conversely, targeting lower prices expands the pool of potential buyers, but beyond what even $25 billion can reach.
Perhaps a better question is whether the program can help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. As of 2024, California needed to turn 1.35 million renters into homeowners to match the ownership rate in other states. The maximum 17% support for entry-level homes would have gotten the state about 41% of the way there. Maximum support for the maximum price would have barely made a dent (8%), while the lower five percent support for entry-level homes would have more than closed the gap (136%).
If Prop 37 passes, it will face additional barriers. Many renters would clearly fail to qualify for a conventional mortgage even with the down payment assistance, and many others might not be able to come up with any money for a down payment at all. Moreover, because the money must be spent on newly-built homes, the proposition’s success depends on builders expanding housing inventory.
At the same time, Prop 37’s $25 billion could meaningfully help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. The key will be to target, to the extent possible under the rules of the program, homes that are well below the maximum price allowed. Prop 37 might help Californians buy a home, but its dollars must spread across a larger number of lower-spending recipients to have the biggest effect.

Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?

By Ben Christopher, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.

It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.

It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country. 

There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37. 

Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.

Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers. 

Q: What would Proposition 37 do?

A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.

$25 billion? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget.

It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything. 

When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 and 38, would be paid back directly with tax dollars.

With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest. 

If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults. 

Are these loans just home mortgages?

Second mortgages, specifically.

Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.

That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?

Almost all of it. 

The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000. 

Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?

Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest or lowest homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it. 

For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn't going to help. 

But for some, it's the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey. The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.

Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview. 

Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?

He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California political debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.

Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.

If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?

If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible. 

Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters, according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis. 

Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify. 

There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income, first-generation or veteran homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said. 

But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California, worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.  

That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities. 

What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?

Two conditions apply.

First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.

Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.

Why only new homes?

This gets at a common critique of down payment assistance programs. 

Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.

Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.

Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.

How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?

It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.

To encourage the industry to build eligible homes, the measure includes a “qualified builder” option. If a builder agrees to abide by the measure’s price cap and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements, they’re shielded from construction defect lawsuits as long as they repair any future mistakes to a homeowner's satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.

The actual number of new units depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a whole bunch of other unknowns.

What other unknowns?

There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure. 

We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans. 

Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?

Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn't come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.

Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.

Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7%. Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.

That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.
